1G OurBigBook.com
For every prime number p with n<p≤2n, the numerator (2n)! contains one factor p, whereas neither copy of n! contains one. Consequently the product of these prime numbers divides the binomial coefficient (n2n​). Since this binomial coefficient is one positive summand of ∑j=02n​(j2n​)=22n, and other summands are positive,
θ(2n)−θ(n)=log∏n<p≤2n​p≤log(n2n​)<2nlog2.
(1)
For x≥2, choose k with 2k−1<x≤2k. The Chebyshev function is increasing, so telescoping gives
θ(x)≤θ(2k)=∑j=1k​(θ(2j)−θ(2j−1))<(2k+1−2)log2<4xlog2.
(2)
For x=1 the inequality follows from θ(1)=0. Thus θ(x)<4(log2)x​ throughout the stated range.

a OurBigBook.com
For n≥3, extend the restriction of the continuous function f to [1/n,1−1/n] to a continuous function fn​ on [0,1] by making it constant on each of the two remaining intervals. The Weierstrass approximation theorem supplies a polynomial Pn​ with ∥Pn​−fn​∥∞,[0,1]​<1/n. Every compact set K⊂(0,1) is eventually contained in [1/n,1−1/n], where fn​=f. Hence supK​∣Pn​−f∣<1/n eventually. This proves uniform convergence on every compact subset, without assuming any endpoint limits of f. The first two polynomials can be chosen arbitrarily.

Write M=sup(0,1)​∣f∣<∞ and use the same constant extensions fn​ as in part (a). They satisfy ∥fn​∥∞​≤M. Choose polynomials Qn​ with ∥Qn​−fn​∥∞​<1/n for n≥3, and set the first two polynomials equal to zero. Then nsup​0<x<1sup​∣Qn​(x)∣≤M+1​, while the argument of part (a) proves uniform convergence to f on every compact subset of (0,1). The bound concerns the entire interval, rather than just each separate compact subset.

3F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 153 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 153
3F OurBigBook.com
Consider the Möbius transformations
A(z)=z+2,B(z)=2z+1z​,A=(10​21​),B=(12​01​).
(3)
Their group lies in PSL2​(Z), which is a discrete subgroup of the Möbius group: integer entries cannot approach the identity matrix except by eventually equalling it, and passing to the quotient by {I,−I} preserves this property.
For freeness let X={x∈R:∣x∣>1} and Y={x∈R:∣x∣<1}. For every nonzero integer n, An(Y)=(2n−1,2n+1)⊂X and
Bn(x)=2nx+1x​,∣Bn(x)∣=∣2n+1/x∣1​<1(x∈X).
(4)
A reduced word involving both generators can be conjugated to a cyclically reduced word beginning with An and ending with a nonzero power of B, after interchanging the generators if necessary. Repeated use of these inclusions shows that this word sends X into the proper subset An(Y) of X, so it cannot be the identity. Nonzero pure powers of either generator are also nonidentity. This is the ping-pong lemma in this particular action, and proves that ⟨A,B⟩≅F2​​ is a free group of rank two as well as a discrete subgroup of PSL2​(C).

4H (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 159 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 159
4H OurBigBook.com
Use the binary Hamming code C=kerH⊂F215​, where the jth column hj​ of the 4×15 parity-check matrix H is the four-digit binary expansion of j, for 1≤j≤15. Thus the columns are precisely the nonzero vectors of F24​. They include the four coordinate vectors, so rankH=4 and dimC=15−4=11. Its code rate is therefore 11/15​.
For a received word y, compute its syndrome s=Hy. If s=0, report no error. Otherwise identify the unique column hj​=s and flip bit j. Indeed, if y=c+ej​ with c∈C, then Hy=Hc+Hej​=hj​, so this procedure recovers c exactly. No column is zero and no two columns coincide; hence no nonzero codeword has Hamming weight one or two. Some three columns sum to zero, for example those indexed by 1,2,3, so the minimum distance is exactly three. Thus every single-bit error is corrected. The assertion requires at most one error; arbitrary multiple errors need not be detected by this procedure.

For the three scalar coefficients, the corresponding columns are 1,x1​,x2​. The necessary and sufficient conditions are
i=1∑n​xi1​=0,i=1∑n​xi2​=0,i=1∑n​xi1​xi2​=0.​
(5)
Under the assumed full rank, neither explanatory column is zero. The maximum-likelihood estimator is β​=(XTX)−1XTY, and the normal distribution of Y implies
β​∼N3​(β,σ2diag(n1​,∑i​xi12​1​,∑i​xi22​1​)).
(6)
Thus the three coefficient estimators are independent normal random variables, not merely uncorrelated. This is a sampling-distribution statement with the true σ2 fixed.

6A OurBigBook.com
Let pjn​ be the probability of occupying site ja after n steps, with pj0​=1{j=0}​ and α+β=1. The master equation is
pjn+1​=αpj−1n​+βpj+1n​.​
(7)
Write pjn​≈ap(ja,nτ) so that the limiting p is a probability density. A Taylor expansion of this master equation gives
τpt​=(β−α)apx​+2(α+β)a2​pxx​+O(a3,τ2).
(8)
The weakly biased diffusion limit of a weakly biased random walk keeps a2/τ and (α−β)a/τ finite as a,τ→0, so α−β=O(a). The limiting advection-diffusion equation is
pt​+Vpx​=Dpxx​,V=τa(α−β)​,D=2τa2(α+β)​=2τa2​.​
(9)
Its initial condition is the Dirac delta function at the origin. At finite spacing, the exact variance gained per step is a2[1−(α−β)2]=4a2αβ. Thus a finite-step central limit theorem gives the variance-matched coefficient 2a2αβ/τ; its difference from the displayed D vanishes in the stated weak-bias diffusion limit of a weakly biased random walk. Keeping a fixed nonzero bias while taking diffusive space-time scaling would instead make V diverge.

7E OurBigBook.com
The fixed points satisfy x[rx(1−x)−1]=0. There is always x=0, and the other branches are
x±​(r)=21±1−4/r​​,r≥4.
(10)
They coincide at (r,x)=(4,1/2). For 0<x<1, F(x)>0 and its maximum occurs at x=2/3, with value 4r/27. Consequently F((0,1))⊂(0,1)⟺0<r<27/4​; equality at the upper endpoint fails because the maximum is attained inside the interval.
The fixed-point multiplier at zero is zero, so zero is attracting for every r>0. On either nonzero branch,
F′(x)=1−x2−3x​.
(11)
The lower branch has multiplier greater than one for r>4 and is repelling. The upper branch is attracting for 4<r<16/3, reaches multiplier −1 at x=3/4, and is repelling for r>16/3. At r=4 the multiplier is +1, and the two branches are created in a saddle-node bifurcation. The fixed point there is attracting from one side and repelling from the other: F(x)−x=−4x(x−1/2)2.
The second change is a supercritical period-doubling bifurcation at (r,x)=(16/3,3/4)​. To check its type, expand at that fixed point. The local map has quadratic coefficient a=−20/3 and cubic coefficient b=−16/3 when the multiplier is −1. Its second iterate has cubic coefficient −2(a2+b)=−704/9<0. The multiplier decreases through −1 as r increases, so a small attracting two-cycle is born on the r>16/3 side. These exhaust the fixed-point bifurcations, since their multipliers have no other crossings of ±1.

8B (Further Complex Methods)

Solution

Words: 230
8B OurBigBook.com
First suppose the integral of g(ξ)/(ξ−z) converges, for example if g∈L1(R). Substitute the complexified coordinates x=(z+aˉ)/2, y=(z−aˉ)/(2i) into the Poisson integral. The factorization of its denominator gives
2u(2z+aˉ​,2iz−aˉ​)=iπ1​∫R​g(ξ)(ξ−z1​−ξ−aˉ1​)dξ.
(12)
The given Schwarz integral formula therefore writes f(z) as (iπ)−1∫g(ξ)/(ξ−z)dξ plus a constant. For z=x+iy, the real part of this integral is exactly the Poisson integral, since
Rei(ξ−z)1​=(ξ−x)2+y2y​.
(13)
The remaining constant has zero real part, giving f(z)=(iπ)−1∫R​ξ−zg(ξ)​dξ+ic​ with c∈R. The complex substitution is initially understood where the real-analytic harmonic function has its complexification; the holomorphic integral then continues the identity throughout the upper half-plane.
Decay of u alone does not guarantee convergence of the printed unregularized integral. For example, choose a continuous g which vanishes on (−∞,e] and equals 1/logξ for ξ≥e2, with continuous interpolation. It is bounded and tends to zero at both ends. Its Poisson integral tends to zero as ∣z∣→∞ in the closed upper half-plane: split the boundary function into a small uniform tail and a compactly supported part. Nevertheless ∫∞g(ξ)/(ξ−z)dξ diverges like loglogξ, even as a symmetric principal value. With only the stated decay assumptions, the always convergent version is
f(z)=iπ1​∫R​g(ξ)(ξ−z1​−1+ξ2ξ​)dξ+ic.​
(14)
The subtracted kernel is real on the integration line, so it changes only the imaginary constant and leaves the harmonic function u unchanged. The kernel difference is O(ξ−2), which ensures convergence for bounded g.

I3​=ρ∫−h/2h/2​dz∫0a​r3dr∫02π​dθ=2Ma2​.

Set I=I1​=I2​. The third of the Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body gives I3​ω˙3​=0, so ω3​ is constant. Define Ω=(I3​−I)ω3​/I. The first two Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body become
ω˙1​=−Ωω2​,ω˙2​=Ωω1​,
(17)
so ω1​+iω2​=CeiΩt. Since the body-frame angular momentum has components (Iω1​,Iω2​,I3​ω3​), its transverse components rotate at Ω while its axial component is constant. Substitution of the principal moments of inertia gives
Ω=3a2+h23a2−h2​ω3​.​
(18)
This is precession relative to the body axes; the angular momentum is constant in an inertial frame. If h2=3a2, the rate is zero even when ω3​=0. If the transverse components vanish, the precession cone degenerates to its axis.

a OurBigBook.com
Assemble the star by adding spherical shells. A shell of mass dm at radius r has gravitational potential energy −Gm(r)dm/r relative to infinity, giving
Egrav​=−∫0R​rGm(r)​dm=−4πG∫0R​m(r)ρ(r)rdr.​
(19)
Multiplication of the hydrostatic equilibrium equation by 4πr3 and integration by parts gives
Egrav​=∫0R​4πr3P′(r)dr=4πR3P(R)−3∫V​PdV.
(20)
For an isolated star with negligible surface pressure, P(R)=0. Using Ekin​=(3/2)∫V​PdV, the virial theorem becomes 2Ekin​+Egrav​=0​. If a nonzero external pressure is present, the surface term must be retained: 2Ekin​+Egrav​=3P(R)V. Thus the printed zero-surface-term identity implicitly assumes an isolated star.

Ekin​=R2α​,α=23​CF​me​h2​(4π3​)2/3(mp​M​)5/3.

In the multiplicative group Fp×​, the squaring map is a group homomorphism with kernel {1,−1}, since p is odd. Every nonzero square therefore has exactly two square roots. There are (p−1)/2 quadratic residues and the same number of nonresidues, and consequently ∑a=1p−1​(pa​)=0.
For nmn​≡1(modp), direct multiplication gives n2(1+mn​)≡n2+n=n(n+1). Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol, including its value zero on multiples of p, implies
(pn(n+1)​)=(p1+mn​​).
(24)
Inversion permutes Fp×​, so 1+mn​ runs through all residue classes except 1. Thus
n=1∑p−1​(pn(n+1)​)=a∈Fp​, a=1∑​(pa​)=0−1=−1.​

a OurBigBook.com
The polynomial form of the Runge approximation theorem says: if K⊂C is compact, C∖K is connected, and f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of K, then for every ε>0 there is a polynomial P with supK​∣f−P∣<ε. Choosing errors tending to zero gives a uniformly convergent sequence of polynomials. Equivalently, on an open domain with connected complement in the Riemann sphere, every holomorphic function is the compact-uniform limit of polynomials. The connected-complement hypothesis excludes enclosed holes containing poles of the function being approximated.

b

Words: 118 Articles: 1
12F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 118
b OurBigBook.com
A compact set K⊂C has exactly one unbounded complementary component, since its complement contains the outside of a sufficiently large disk. The connected, unbounded open set Ω, being disjoint from K, lies in that component. In particular ζ belongs to the unbounded component.
Fill all bounded components of C∖K to obtain the polynomial hull K. It is a compact set with connected complement, and ζ∈/K. Therefore 1/(z−ζ) is holomorphic on a neighborhood of K. The Runge approximation theorem gives polynomials Pn​ converging uniformly to this function on K, hence on K. This proves the requested uniform polynomial approximation on K, even when K itself has holes. If K is empty, the assertion is vacuous.

0=limn​∫∣z∣=1​Pn​(z)dz=∫∣z∣=1​zdz​=2πi,
(26)
a contradiction to the Cauchy integral theorem. Thus boundedness of this Ω permits the obstruction excluded in part (b).

Solution

Words: 199
13A OurBigBook.com
The species u is the activator, since increasing u increases its own production u2/v; v is the inhibitor, since increasing v reduces that production. The unique positive uniform steady state solves v=u2 and u2/v=bu, giving u∗​=1/b, v∗​=1/b2​.
The reaction Jacobian matrix at this state is
J=(b2/b​−b2−1​),trJ=b−1,detJ=b.
(27)
Its eigenvalues solve λ2+(1−b)λ+b=0. Since b>0, both have negative real part precisely for 0<b<1. This proves stability of the spatially uniform reaction kinetics.
A perturbation proportional to eλt+ikx replaces J by J−k2diag(1,d). Put q=k2. Its trace is b−1−(1+d)q<0 in the kinetically stable range, and its determinant is
D(q)=dq2+(1−bd)q+b.
(28)
A growing spatial mode exists exactly when this determinant is negative for some q>0. Its minimum occurs at q=(bd−1)/(2d), which is positive only if bd>1, and the minimum is negative precisely if (bd−1)2>4bd. Together these conditions reduce to the Turing threshold of the quadratic activator-inhibitor model,
0<b<1,bd>3+22​.​
(29)
The unstable band is
2dbd−1−(bd−1)2−4bd​​<k2<2dbd−1+(bd−1)2−4bd​​.
(30)
At the Turing instability threshold the band shrinks to its double root, yielding kc2​=(1+2​)/d​. On a bounded spatial interval, an allowed wavenumber must additionally lie in the unstable band; the displayed parameter condition assumes the continuous spatial spectrum.

Put s=b​. The two fixed points on the invariant line x=0 are P+​=(0,s) and P−​=(0,−s). There are also Q±​=(±b−a2/4​,−a/2) when a2<4b. At equality they coalesce with P−​.
The Jacobian matrix is
J(x,y)=(−a−2y2x​−2x2y​).
(31)
At P+​ its eigenvalues are −a−2s and 2s, so it is always a saddle equilibrium. At P−​ they are 2s−a and −2s, so it is a saddle equilibrium for a<2s and a stable node for a>2s, with a zero eigenvalue at a=2s.
At Q±​ the characteristic equation is λ2+aλ+4b−a2=0, giving
λ=2−a±5a2−16b​​.
(32)
For 0<a2<16b/5 these points are stable spirals; for 16b/5<a2<4b they are stable nodes. At a2=16b/5 the double negative eigenvalue has only one independent eigenvector, so these are improper stable nodes. When a=0 they are center equilibria, as established in part (iii). Thus the collision at a2=4b>0​ changes both the number and stability of fixed points; it is the bifurcation classified below.

Set Y=y+s and μ=2s−a, and include μ˙​=0 for the extended center manifold. The equations near P−​ become
x˙=μx−2xY,Y˙=x2−2sY+Y2,μ˙​=0.

The stable direction has eigenvalue −2s and the center directions are (x,μ). Choose a symmetry-preserving center manifold Y=h(x,μ), even in x, containing the equilibrium line x=0,Y=0. Its invariance equation is
hx​(μx−2xh)=x2−2sh+h2.
(34)
Write h=Ax2+Bμx2+⋯. At degree two, 0=(1−2sA)x2, so A=1/(2s). At degree three, 2Aμx2=−2sBμx2, so B=−1/(2s2). Consequently
x˙=μx−sx3​+O(μx3,x5).
(35)
With x=s​X this is X˙=μX−X3+O(μX3,X5), the supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. For μ<0, P−​ is attracting; for μ>0 it becomes a saddle equilibrium and two attracting branches appear, consistent with the exact Q±​.
For 0<a2<4b, the vertical invariant line flows from P+​ towards P−​ between those points. The two off-axis stable equilibria lie below the horizontal axis, one in each invariant half-plane x>0 and x<0. For a2>4b, these stable equilibria have merged into the stable node P−​, while P+​ remains a saddle equilibrium. Filled green points mark attracting equilibria, green rings mark centers, and red crosses mark saddle equilibria. The plotted arrows and nullclines show the corresponding phase portraits; a focus can become a node within the first parameter range without changing the pitchfork classification.

Small regular level curves around either point are closed curves, and the vector field is nonzero on them. The separatrix level is H=0, consisting of x=0 and x2/3+y2=b. The two arcs of this ellipse run from the lower saddle equilibrium to the upper one, while the vertical segment runs from the upper saddle to the lower one. They enclose the two families of periodic orbits, as shown in the last panel of the phase portrait. Outside the loops, regular levels are unbounded.
For a>0 the divergence of the original vector field is exactly −a. If a periodic orbit existed, uniqueness of trajectories would make it a simple closed curve, tangent everywhere to the vector field. The flux across its boundary would be zero, whereas the divergence theorem would give −a times its positive enclosed area. This contradiction is the Bendixson-Dulac criterion. Hence periodic orbits exist if and only if a=0​.

The induced ordering on x is a well-order. By transfinite recursion define h(t)={h(s):s∈x, s<t} for t∈x. Induction shows that each h(t) is an ordinal, that these values strictly increase, and that their range is the ordinal μ(x)=⋃t∈x​(h(t)+1). The map h is an order isomorphism from x to this ordinal. The Brooks' theorem states that a finite connected simple graph with maximum vertex degree Δ has chromatic number at most Δ, unless it is a complete graph or an odd cycle graph; those exceptions have chromatic number Δ+1.
First, if the graph is not regular, choose a vertex v of degree less than Δ and a spanning tree rooted at v. Order vertices with every child before its parent, and apply the greedy coloring algorithm. Every vertex except v has an as-yet uncolored parent, so has at most Δ−1 colored neighbors; v also has fewer than Δ neighbors. Thus Δ colors suffice. This justifies reducing to the regular case.
Now let G be regular, 3-connected and not complete. A shortest path between two nonadjacent vertices contains an induced two-edge path a,v,b with a,b nonadjacent. By 3-connectivity, G−{a,b} is connected. Color a,b with the same color. Choose a spanning tree of the remaining graph rooted at v and color its vertices in child-before-parent order. Each vertex other than v again has an uncolored parent and thus at most Δ−1 already colored neighbors. At the last vertex v, the two neighbors a,b share a color, so its Δ neighbors use at most Δ−1 distinct colors. A color is therefore available at every step, proving χ(G)≤Δ​ in the required 3-connected noncomplete case. A 3-connected graph has Δ≥3, so the odd-cycle exception cannot arise here.

For a compact space K, the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem says that a family F⊂C(K) is relatively compact in the supremum norm if and only if it is pointwise bounded and equicontinuous. In the usual formulation K is compact Hausdorff; the elementary argument below also works for any compact K for real-valued continuous functions.
Pointwise bounded means supf∈F​∣f(x)∣<∞ for every x∈K. Equicontinuity means that for every x∈K and ε>0 there is a neighborhood U of x such that ∣f(y)−f(x)∣<ε for every y∈U and f∈F. Relative compactness means compactness of the closure in C(K), where ∥f∥∞​=supK​∣f∣. This is a complete metric vector space, since uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous. Equivalently, every sequence in the family has a uniformly convergent subsequence, with limit in C(K), though not necessarily in the original family.

Assume first that F is compact in the supremum norm. A finite norm-net shows that the norms of its members are bounded, so pointwise boundedness follows. Given x and ε>0, choose a finite ε/3-net g1​,…,gN​ in the closure. Their continuity gives a common neighborhood U of x where ∣gj​(y)−gj​(x)∣<ε/3 for every j. For any f∈F, choose gj​ with ∥f−gj​∥∞​<ε/3; the triangle inequality then gives ∣f(y)−f(x)∣<ε. Thus the family is equicontinuous.
Conversely, suppose pointwise boundedness and equicontinuity. For a prescribed ε>0, choose neighborhoods Ux​ where every f varies from f(x) by less than ε/3. Compactness supplies a finite subcover Ux1​​,…,UxN​​. Pointwise boundedness makes the set of vectors (f(x1​),…,f(xN​)) bounded in RN. Partition a bounding box into finitely many boxes of coordinate diameter less than ε/3, and choose one function from each occupied box. If f,g belong to the same box and y∈Uxj​​, then
∣f(y)−g(y)∣≤∣f(y)−f(xj​)∣+∣f(xj​)−g(xj​)∣+∣g(xj​)−g(y)∣<ε.
(48)
The chosen functions are therefore a finite ε-net in the supremum norm. Thus F is totally bounded. Its closure is complete and totally bounded, hence compact. To recall the last metric-space fact, successively selecting subsequences in balls of radii 2−j produces a Cauchy diagonal subsequence from every sequence; completeness supplies its limit. This proves both directions of the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem.

Two function elements (U,f) and (V,g) define the same germ of a holomorphic function at p when p∈U∩V and they agree on some neighborhood of p. Write the germ as [f]p​. Basic open sets of the space of germs of holomorphic functions are
Uf​={[f]p​:p∈U},
(49)
for open U on which f is holomorphic. If two such sets meet, equality of the germs gives a smaller open sheet contained in their intersection, so these sets form a basis. The projection π([f]p​)=p maps each sheet homeomorphically onto U. Compose this with a local coordinate on X to define the complex charts on the germ space. Transition maps are the corresponding transition maps on X, hence holomorphic; π is a local biholomorphism and is onto, since even constant functions provide germs over every point.
The germ space is Hausdorff. Germs over different points are separated by base neighborhoods. For distinct germs over the same point, choose representatives on one small connected disk. If their two sheets met anywhere in that disk, the representatives would agree on an open set and hence everywhere on the disk by the identity theorem, a contradiction. These sheets thus separate the germs. Together with the allowed second-countability fact, the charts make each component a Riemann surface.
Here “covering in the sense of complex analysis” means this locally biholomorphic, possibly incomplete analytic germ projection. It does not mean an evenly covered topological covering map: an analytic branch can cease to exist at a singularity, so the restriction to a component need not project onto all of X.
The evaluation map E([f]p​)=f(p) is holomorphic, since on the sheet Uf​ it is just f. Starting from one germ, continuation through overlapping disks produces exactly the germs in its connected component. Indeed such continuations give paths in the germ space; conversely, cover a path by finitely many successive sheets to obtain a chain of function elements. Components are path-connected because the surface is locally path-connected. No two distinct germs can be added to that component without being obtainable by continuation. It therefore represents the maximal analytic continuation, or complete holomorphic function, of any of its germs. Conversely every such maximal continuation embeds into the germ space by taking its local germs; completeness makes its image the entire component. These constructions are inverse, giving the requested bijection between complete holomorphic functions and connected components, with functions understood up to their natural equivalence as analytic continuations, rather than merely as single-valued functions defined on all of X.

For a divisor on an algebraic curve D, let L(D)=H0(V,O(D)) and choose a basis of dimension r+1. Regarding the basis as sections of the divisor line bundle, evaluation gives ϕD​:V→Pr. If the linear system of divisors has no base points, at least one section is nonzero at each point, and these homogeneous coordinates define a morphism. If the effective divisor has a fixed part F, first divide all sections by their common vanishing factor. The moving divisor E=D−F is base-point-free, has the same section space, and gives the uniquely extended morphism on the smooth curve. Thus effectiveness alone does not make the raw evaluations everywhere nonzero, but cancellation supplies the usual map.
A morphism from a projective integral curve is a finite morphism onto its image precisely when it is nonconstant, equivalently r≥1: a positive-dimensional fiber of a curve would be the whole curve, while a nonconstant proper map with finite fibers is finite. It is an isomorphism onto its image precisely when its moving complete linear system is very ample. In section-space terms, putting h=h0(E), the criteria are
h0(E−P)=h−1for all P,h0(E−P−Q)=h−2for all P,Q,
(50)
where Q=P is allowed. These express absence of base points, separation of distinct points, and separation of tangent directions. In the base-point-free convention E=D.
Now suppose the genus is two. The Riemann-Roch theorem gives degK=2 and h0(K)=2. There cannot be a nonconstant function with only a single simple pole on a positive-genus smooth projective curve: it would give a degree-one map to P1, an isomorphism. Hence h0(P)=1 for every point P. Applying Riemann-Roch theorem to K−P gives h0(K−P)=h0(P)=1, so the canonical linear system has no base point. The resulting map ϕK​:V→P1 has degree degK=2.
Set D=K+P1​+P2​, of degree four. The Riemann-Roch theorem gives h0(D)=3 and h0(D−P)=2 for every P, since the residual divisors have negative degree. Thus ϕD​ is a base-point-free map to P2 with nondegenerate image C. Degree of the pullback of a general line gives
4=(degϕD​)(degC).
(51)
The image cannot be a line because the three sections are independent. The only alternatives are a birational quartic or a double cover of a conic. In the latter case identify the smooth conic with P1. Its hyperplane bundle has degree two, so D∼2A, where A is a degree-two divisor with h0(A)≥2. Again Riemann-Roch theorem implies h0(K−A)=h0(A)−1≥1. Since K−A has degree zero, it must be linearly equivalent to zero; hence A∼K. This would force P1​+P2​∼K, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore the image is a plane quartic and the map is birational. A smooth plane quartic has genus (4−1)(4−2)/2=3, while its normalization here has genus two. Consequently ϕD​ is birational onto a singular plane quartic​.

For a surface tangent vector, the intrinsic Hessian of h is the normal component of the second fundamental form, namely HessX​h=±b at p. The Hessian is semidefinite because this is a local extremum. Since X is a minimal surface, trg​b=2H=0. A semidefinite symmetric form with zero trace must be zero, so b(p)=0. This makes p a planar point, contradicting the assumption. Therefore X∩Π=∅​.
The boundaryless hypothesis ensures that the minimizing point is an interior surface point. The condition on Dn​ ensures that the infimum is attained; disjointness from a plane alone would not do so.

Tc​=kB​1​[BΓ(9/2)ζ(9/2)N​]2/9.​
(101)
The ground-state population is treated separately from the continuum density of states.

ii OurBigBook.com
Below Tc​ the fugacity is z=1 in the continuum ideal-gas approximation. The zero-energy condensate contributes no internal energy, so the same Bose integral with one additional factor of energy gives
E=BΓ(211​)ζ(211​)(kB​T)11/2.
(102)
Eliminate B using N=BΓ(9/2)ζ(9/2)(kB​Tc​)9/2 and Γ(11/2)=(9/2)Γ(9/2):
E=29​NkB​Tζ(9/2)ζ(11/2)​(Tc​T​)9/2(T≤Tc​).​
(103)
The excited fraction is (T/Tc​)9/2 and the remaining particles occupy the Bose-Einstein condensate. For fixed B, the condensed-state energy at fixed T is independent of how many additional particles are placed in the zero-energy ground state.

iii

Solution

Words: 50
iii OurBigBook.com
In the classical limit the fugacity is small and Lis​(z)=z+O(z2). The Bose-Einstein distribution approaches the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, giving
N≃BzΓ(29​)(kB​T)9/2,E≃BzΓ(211​)(kB​T)11/2.
(104)
Taking the ratio eliminates both z and B, yielding E≃29​NkB​T​. The coefficient 9/2 follows from this density of states, rather than the 3/2 of a free three-dimensional gas.

36C (Electrodynamics)

Words: 176 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 176
36C OurBigBook.com
Use c=1 and metric signature (−,+,+,+), consistent with the supplied rest potential. In the Lorenz gauge, the Maxwell equations reduce to wave equations for the four-potential. A point worldline has current ja(x)=q∫ua(s)δ(4)(x−y(s))ds, where ua=dya/ds. Convolution with the retarded wave Green function θ(R0)δ(R2)/(2π) gives the stated integral: its support is the future light cone of each source point and it excludes incoming advanced signals.
For uniform motion ya(s)=(γs,0,0,γvs), ua=γ(1,0,0,v). Let R=x−y(s). The delta-function argument has derivative d(R2)/ds=−2R⋅u. Only the retarded root survives the step function, so
Aa(x)=4πμ0​q​−R⋅uua​​ret​.
(105)
Put Z=z−vt, r⊥2​=x2+y2, and Δ=t−tret​>0. The light-cone condition is Δ2=r⊥2​+(Z+vΔ)2, whence
Δ=1−v2vZ+Z2+(1−v2)r⊥2​​​,−R⋅u=γ[(1−v2)Δ−vZ]=γZ2+(1−v2)r⊥2​​.
(106)
Therefore, away from the worldline,
ϕ=4π(z−vt)2+(1−v2)(x2+y2)​μ0​q​,Az​=vϕ,Ax​=Ay​=0.​
(107)
As an independent check, in the rest frame z′=γ(z−vt) and r′=x2+y2+γ2Z2​. Its potential is A′a=(μ0​q/(4πr′),0,0,0). A Lorentz transformation gives A0=γA′0, Az=γvA′0, exactly the expression above because r′=γZ2+(1−v2)r⊥2​​. Restoring SI units would require restoring the factors of c in both the four-potential convention and the supplied electrostatic normalization.

37E (Fluid Dynamics II)

Words: 316 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 316
37E OurBigBook.com
For an axisymmetric flow without azimuthal velocity, define the Stokes streamfunction by
uR​=R2sinθΨθ​​,uθ​=−RsinθΨR​​,uϕ​=0.​
(108)
These formulas enforce incompressibility. The only nonzero curl component is R−1[∂R​(Ruθ​)−∂θ​uR​]. Substitution gives
∇×u=(0,0,−RsinθD2Ψ​),D2=∂R2​+R2sinθ​∂θ​(sinθ1​∂θ​).
(109)
Curling the Stokes flow equations eliminates pressure and gives ∇2(∇×u)=0. For an azimuthal field, its vector Laplacian is the scalar Laplacian minus 1/(R2sin2θ); applying that operator to −D2Ψ/(Rsinθ) gives −D2(D2Ψ)/(Rsinθ). Hence the streamfunction equation is D2D2Ψ=0​.
For the proposed sphere solution put f(R)=R2−3aR/2+a3/(2R), so Ψ=(U/2)f(R)sin2θ. Its velocity is
uR​=Ucosθ(1−2R3a​+2R3a3​),uθ​=−Usinθ(1−4R3a​−4R3a3​).
(110)
Both components vanish at R=a and tend to the components of Uez​ at infinity. Also D2Ψ=(U/2)(f′′−2f/R2)sin2θ=(3Ua/(2R))sin2θ, and applying D2 once more gives zero. This verifies the differential equation and both physical boundary conditions.
For a sphere translating upward through otherwise stationary fluid, subtract the uniform background in the sphere frame and reverse its far-flow direction. Its leading disturbance is the upward Stokeslet
u(R)=4R3aU​(I+RRT)ez​+O(Ua3/R3).
(111)
Place an image at z=+d with the opposite, downward velocity −U, while the real sphere is at z=−d. The sum has uz​ odd under z↦−z and ur​ even. Thus at z=0, uz​=0 and ∂z​ur​=0; moreover ∂r​uz​=0. The tangential stress σrz​=μ(∂z​ur​+∂r​uz​) is therefore zero, as required by the stress-free boundary condition.
At a point on the plane with radial coordinate r, the real Stokeslet gives ur​=3aUrd/[4(r2+d2)3/2]. The image gives the same radial contribution, so
ur​(r,0)=2(r2+d2)3/23aUrd​+O(Ud2a2​)(r/d fixed).​
(112)
The surface flow is outward. Although the isolated-sphere dipole term is only O(U(a/d)3), the next correction is O(U(a/d)2): the image's velocity at the real sphere is downward and of size 3aU/(4d), so satisfying the real sphere's prescribed velocity requires a relative O(a/d) correction to its Stokeslet strength. Since the leading surface flow is O(Ua/d), the first reflection already changes it at the displayed second order. Ignoring this boundary-interaction correction would give the wrong next power.

38A (Waves)

Words: 444 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 444
38A OurBigBook.com
Start from ρ(∂t​u+u⋅∇u)=−∇p−ρgez​, ∂t​ρ+u⋅∇ρ=0, and ∇⋅u=0. The stationary background obeys p0′​=−gρ0​. Linearize in small perturbations and use the Boussinesq approximation: replace the density by a reference value ρ∗​ in inertia but retain the density perturbation in the buoyancy force. With π=p′/ρ∗​ and b=−gρ′/ρ∗​,
ut​=−∇π+bez​,bt​+N2w=0,∇⋅u=0,N2=−ρ∗​g​dzdρ0​​>0.​
(113)
This is the Brunt–Väisälä frequency. Its assumed constancy requires a locally uniform stable density gradient in this approximation; rotation and viscosity are neglected.
For a plane wave with wavevector K=(k,ℓ,m), project the momentum equation onto the space perpendicular to K to eliminate pressure. Its vertical component is −iωw=b[1−m2/∣K∣2], while −iωb+N2w=0. Eliminating b yields
ω2=k2+ℓ2+m2N2(k2+ℓ2)​.​
(114)
For 0<ω<N, a small oscillating body radiates upward and downward conical internal gravity wave beams. In a vertical section the beams make a St Andrew's cross, with angle α to the horizontal satisfying sinα=ω/N. Indeed the group velocity is perpendicular to the wavevector and has ratio of vertical to horizontal magnitudes k2+ℓ2​/∣m∣. Thus wave energy follows the cones, rather than the direction normal to a fixed-radius spherical wavefront. There are no such propagating beams for ω>N.
For the shear-flow calculation choose the positive intrinsic-frequency branch and k0​>0, conditions needed for the printed critical-level formula. The slowly varying local dispersion relation is
Ω=kU(z)+ω,ω=k2+m2​Nk​.
(115)
Stationarity and horizontal homogeneity conserve Ω and k=k0​. The Hamiltonian ray equations for a local dispersion relation give
z˙=∂m​Ω=−(k02​+m2)3/2Nk0​m​,m˙=−∂z​Ω=−k0​U′(z)<0.
(116)
Thus m0​<0 stays negative and the ray propagates upward. Conservation of frequency gives
ω(z)=k02​+m02​​Nk0​​−k0​[U(z)−U(0)].
(117)
If the shear reaches the required velocity difference, its first zero is the critical level of an internal gravity wave,
U(zc​)−U(0)=k02​+m02​​N​.​
(118)
As z↑zc​, the intrinsic frequency tends to zero, m→−∞, the vertical wavelength tends to zero and the vertical group velocity tends to zero. The ideal ray cannot cross this level. For finite Uc′​>0, z˙∼k0​(Uc′​)2(zc​−z)2/N, so it approaches the level only asymptotically in time. The disturbance develops short scales; even weak viscosity can then absorb it, and nonlinear effects can invalidate the small-amplitude approximation.
The printed sign and existence hypotheses are incomplete. On the positive-frequency branch, k0​<0 instead gives m˙>0 and eventually a turning point when the intrinsic frequency reaches N. As a concrete counterexample to the stated universal height bound, take N=1, k0​=−1, m0​=−3, and U(z)=εz with any small ε>0. At the printed height zc​=1/(ε10​), the intrinsic frequency is 2/10​<1 and m=−3/2​<0, so the vertical group velocity is still positive and the ray crosses that height. Also, U′>0 alone does not ensure that the displayed velocity difference is ever reached; an increasing bounded U may have no finite critical level. The qualified derivation above gives the intended positive-k0​ result whenever that level exists.

39B (Numerical Analysis)

Words: 313 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 313
39B OurBigBook.com
Set θk​=kπ/(M+1) and extend the proposed vector by v0​=vM+1​=0. For vm​=imsin(mθk​), the angle-addition identity gives
vm+1​−vm−1​=im+1[sin((m+1)θk​)+sin((m−1)θk​)]=2icosθk​vm​.
(119)
Hence the Toeplitz antisymmetric tridiagonal matrix has eigenvalues
λk​=a+2ibcosM+1kπ​,1≤k≤M.​
(120)
The real sine vectors are eigenvectors of the real symmetric tridiagonal matrix with both off-diagonals one, with distinct eigenvalues 2cosθk​; thus they are orthogonal and form a basis. Multiplication by the unitary diagonal matrix diag(i,i2,…,iM) preserves orthogonality. Their squared norms are (M+1)/2, so multiplying by 2/(M+1)​ gives a common orthonormal basis for all a,b, even when some eigenvalues coincide.
Let K have superdiagonal one, subdiagonal minus one and diagonal zero. The prescribed endpoint values remove the exterior unknowns, and the scheme is
B=I−4μ​K,C=I+4μ​K,Bun+1=Cun.​
(121)
In the common orthonormal eigenbasis, the two eigenvalues are 1∓i(μ/2)cosθk​. Every eigenvalue of B is nonzero for real μ, and the amplification matrix Q=B−1C has eigenvalues
qk​=1−i(μ/2)cosθk​1+i(μ/2)cosθk​​,∣qk​∣=1.
(122)
Thus Q is a unitary matrix and ∥un+1∥2​=∥un∥2​ exactly. The same holds for the mesh-weighted norm. This matrix argument proves stability for every real μ, hence every physical μ≥0​, without a Fourier stability calculation.
The printed mesh ratio has a consistency error: advection requires μ=Δt/Δx, while the PDF prints Δt/(Δx)2. Indeed the centered spatial difference is 2Δxux​+O((Δx)3), so division of the scheme by Δt gives leading right-hand coefficient μΔx/Δt. The printed choice makes this 1/Δx rather than one. The stability conclusion is valid for the algebraic scheme with either definition, but does not fix this inconsistency. The continuous first-order advection problem also ordinarily specifies only the inflow endpoint, here x=1; zero data at both endpoints restrict admissible initial data. For example the initially boundary-zero profile sinπx develops nonzero outflow u(0,t)=sinπt before inflow changes reach that boundary. The matrix norm calculation concerns the stated two-endpoint discretization and does not establish well-posedness for arbitrary continuous initial data.
